newsitem.title: USA: East Timor activist urges Clinton to work for peace.
newsitem.headline: East Timor activist urges Clinton to work for peace.

text.p: East Timor activist Jose Ramos-Horta, in his first U.S. appearance since jointly winning the Nobel Peace Prize, on Tuesday urged President Bill Clinton to become personally involved in negotiating peace for the Indonesian-ruled territory.

Ramos-Horta, who held a news conference in New York as four activists sought political asylum in Europe, accused Jakarta of waging a campaign to prevent fellow peace laureate, the Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo, from travelling to Oslo in December to receive his award.

"I'm optimistic that some time next year, when the Indonesians recover from the psychological therapy from the Nobel committee, when they wake up to the reality, they probably will negotiate much more seriously," said Ramos-Horta, joint winner of the prize with Bishop Belo last month.
The former Portuguese colony has been a focal point for trouble since Indonesian troops invaded in November 1975 and Indonesia absorbed the territory as its 27th province the following July.

The United Nations recognises Portugal as the administering power and years of U.N.-sponsored negotiations between Jakarta and Lisbon failed to settle the issue. Ramos-Horta, self-exiled resistance spokesman for East Timor, told reporters he did not expect any breakthroughs in the ninth round of talks scheduled for December.

He did say however, "I'm more optimistic for 1997, particularly if President Clinton takes it as a personal issue that he cherishes and that he can resolve much more quickly and easily than the Middle East or Bosnia."

The peace prize winner, who humbly quipped that he was more deserving of an award from the International Association of Travel Agents for the many miles he has flown as a spokesman for the East Timor independence movement, planned to visit Washington on Wednesday.
There were speaking engagements on his agenda, but no meetings with Clinton administration officials.
In Jakarta on Tuesday, 2,000 members of the youth wing of the ruling Golkar party demonstrated in front of parliament, calling for Bishop Belo's expulsion from Indonesia.

Ramos-Horta said the demonstration was part of a government campaign to question Belo's loyalty and citizenship and withdraw his passport. He said Jakarta wanted to force Belo to apply for a passport from Portugal or the Vatican in order to travel to Olso and that he would then need a visa to return to Indonesia.

In other developments, four men from East Timor sought political asylum in the Spanish embassy in Jakarta and students staged a brief protest on the fifth anniversary of the killings of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor.

Indonesian troops killed the demonstrators on Nov. 12, 1991, after a funeral for an anti-Indonesian activist in Dili, East Timor, according to an official report. Witnesses and human rights groups estimated at least 180 people died.
Portugal has granted political asylum to 89 East Timorese who have entered foreign missions in Jakarta since September 1995.
